solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Youngster I start to lecture?

parts.note: a pup is a young animal, and by extension a cheeky young person

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only the first letter of lecture is used

explanation.surface: A young person nervously announces that they are about to give a talk.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines the answer: one being lectured is a learner, a youngster who could say 'I start to lecture?' with puzzlement.
explanation.definitionFit: A school pupil is a young learner, the one a teacher's lecture is aimed at.

clue.text: Flying vehicle on flight, finally, for Mars?

parts.note: an aeroplane, or plane, is a vehicle that flies

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word flight

explanation.surface: An aircraft taking off, with the question of whether it might reach Mars.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks Mars as an example: it is one of the worlds orbiting the Sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Mars is the fourth world from the Sun, an example of the class of heavenly body asked for.

clue.text: Measure of importance under the mistletoe?

definitions.text: Measure of importance under the mistletoe?

parts.words: Measure of importance under the mistletoe?
parts.note: a ranking of status, read playfully as the sequence of kisses (pecks) given under the mistletoe

explanation.surface: A wry look at who gets kissed first under the Christmas mistletoe.
explanation.walkthrough: A peck is a quick kiss, so a 'measure of importance under the mistletoe' could be the order in which people are pecked; the real phrase is a social hierarchy.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the hierarchy of rank in a group, first observed among hens pecking each other.

clue.text: Literary giant ruined pursuing legal action

parts.note: lit is the common short form for literary, as in English Lit

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked out of shape, so these letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A great author has been brought low by a lawsuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literary giant' looks like one phrase meaning a great writer; it splits, with 'ruined' rearranging only the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: A litigant is a party engaged in a lawsuit, so the word describes someone taking a case to court.

clue.text: Arachnid runs underneath piano in bank

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece underneath another comes after it
in places the piano letter within the word for the bank

parts.note: a bank of a river is one of its sides
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly
R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A spider scuttles about under a piano on a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: P goes inside SIDE to make SPIDE; 'underneath' puts R below it in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An arachnid is an eight-legged creature, and the web-spinner is the best-known example of the class.

clue.text: Forestall reduced group of countries

indicators.note: reduced means cut down, so the word for forestall loses its last letter

parts.note: to forestall something is to block it

explanation.surface: An alliance of nations has been cut back to prevent something.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloc is an alliance of nations or parties acting together, such as the old Eastern bloc.

clue.text: Road vehicle adopted by one American guy involved in fatal flight

indicators.note: adopted by means taken in, so the car goes inside the other letters

parts.note: the Roman numeral I stands for one
a car is a vehicle driven on the road

explanation.surface: A man in an American car, linked somehow to a deadly air journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adopted by' means taken in, so the vehicle sits inside the letters for one and American.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Icarus flew on wings of wax and feathers, went too near the Sun and fell to his death in the sea.

clue.text: I'm leading a lot of constables to capture it? Unwise

indicators.note: leading means coming in front, so these letters start the answer

parts.note: taken as written, losing only its apostrophe

indicators.note: to capture is to take hold of, so the shortened police letters go round it
a lot of means most but not all, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: constables are members of the police

explanation.surface: Someone boasting about heading a team of officers to arrest something, then calling it unwise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lot of' trims the last letter, leaving POLIC; 'to capture' then takes in the word it, and 'leading' puts I'm first.
explanation.definitionFit: Impolitic describes an action that is not sensible or prudent in the circumstances.

clue.text: Variety of top celestial or astronomical event

indicators.note: a variety of the letters means some different arrangement of them

explanation.surface: Choose between a fine heavenly sight and an astronomical happening.
explanation.definitionFit: When the Moon wholly hides the Sun, observers see a rare and dramatic event in the sky.

clue.text: A visitor from Edinburgh, say, in Berkshire town

parts.note: someone from Edinburgh is a Scot; 'say' marks this as one example

explanation.surface: A tourist from Scotland's capital spending time in an English county town.
explanation.walkthrough: Berkshire is an English county west of London; Ascot is famous for its royal racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a town in Berkshire, England, best known for its racecourse and Royal Ascot meeting.

clue.text: Elected tyrant, not the first time? That's a sign

parts.note: a party that is elected is in power

indicators.note: the letter T stands for time; the first one is dropped from the word

parts.note: a dictator is a tyrannical ruler

explanation.surface: An elected ruler turning despotic again, taken as a warning sign.
explanation.walkthrough: T stands for time, so 'not the first time' removes the first T of DICTATOR, leaving DICATOR.
explanation.definitionFit: An indicator is something that points to or shows a condition, much as a sign does.

clue.text: Money fool returned

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the word for fool is read from the end

parts.note: a nit, or nitwit, is a fool

explanation.surface: A foolish person got their cash back.
explanation.definitionFit: Tin is an old slang term for cash, from the metal coins once made of base metal.

clue.text: Disorganised carpool is a sight to see in Athens

definitions.text: a sight to see in Athens

indicators.note: something disorganised is in a jumble, so these letters are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: A chaotic car-sharing trip to visit a tourist attraction in Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: The Acropolis is the ancient citadel above Athens, home of the Parthenon and a major tourist attraction.

clue.text: Finished source of mutton before one serving of ham

indicators.note: in a down clue, before means this piece comes ahead of the next

parts.note: something finished is past
mutton is the meat of sheep, here from a ram
the Roman numeral I stands for one

explanation.surface: A meal: lamb finished, ham dish to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: pastrami is usually spiced cured beef, but like ham it is cured, smoked meat served sliced.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastrami is cured, smoked meat sliced thin like ham, so a portion of it is a cold-cut serving.

clue.text: Looking peculiar in soccer gear? Every chance!

indicators.note: in places the word for peculiar inside the word for soccer gear

parts.note: footballers wear shorts
peculiar means odd

explanation.surface: Someone looks strange in their football kit, and the outcome is all but certain.
explanation.definitionFit: Betting at short odds means the bookmaker thinks the outcome very likely, so there is every chance of it.

clue.text: Pacific islands are home to small spicy dish

indicators.note: to be home to something is to hold it inside, so the islands surround the letter for small

parts.note: Samoa is a group of islands in the South Pacific
S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: South Sea islands where a little hot meal is served.
explanation.definitionFit: A samosa is a fried pastry triangle filled with spiced vegetables or meat, a South Asian snack.

clue.text: Spot mature time of feeble-mindedness

parts.note: a dot is a small spot
to age is to mature, as wine or cheese does

explanation.surface: Seeing signs of ripening in someone growing old and confused.
explanation.definitionFit: Dotage is the period of weakened faculties that can come with old age.

clue.text: Pet fur has nothing removed

indicators.note: removed means taken out, so the letter for nothing leaves the word for fur

parts.note: an animal's fur is its coat
O looks like zero, meaning nothing

explanation.surface: An animal's fur that has not been shed at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'has nothing removed' as 'is intact'; instead O, nothing, is taken out of COAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat is one of the commonest household animals kept for companionship.

clue.text: Sign of gratitude, having supplied skill

parts.note: ta is an informal British word for thank you
to lend is to supply for a time, so supplied gives lent

explanation.surface: A thank-you for providing someone with ability.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is British slang for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Talent is a natural aptitude or gift for doing something well.

clue.text: Irrational character had gone wrong in the topic

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the word for topic

parts.note: the matter is the subject in hand

indicators.note: something gone wrong is out of order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A muddled thinker whose argument has gone off the rails on the subject at hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gone wrong' rearranges had into ADH, and 'in' sets those letters inside the word for topic, just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mad Hatter is Lewis Carroll's nonsensical tea-party host in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.

clue.text: One opposing article returned it

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the word it is read in reverse

explanation.surface: A dissenter sending back a newspaper item.
explanation.definitionFit: An anti is a person who is against a policy or idea, the opposite of a pro.

clue.text: Enough to taste? Not initially

indicators.note: not initially means the word loses its first letter

parts.note: to sample food is to taste it

explanation.surface: A cook judges whether there is enough food, without trying it first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not initially' drops the S from SAMPLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample means plentiful or more than sufficient for what is needed.

clue.text: Matt rages after changing plan

indicators.note: after changing describes the letters once altered, so they are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Matt flies into a fury once the arrangements are altered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after changing' looks like a time phrase in the story but signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A stratagem is a cunning scheme devised to achieve an aim.

clue.text: One trap set around river still

parts.note: the Roman numeral I stands for one

indicators.note: set around means placed surrounding, so the net goes round the river letter

parts.note: a net is used to trap fish or animals
R is the standard abbreviation for river on maps

explanation.surface: Someone lays a trap beside a river and keeps quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: Inert means motionless, without movement or action.
